Contributing to fleet

Source: CONTRIBUTING.md

fleet is a deterministic mean-field counterpart to the malariasimulation individual-based model (IBM), advanced one day at a time on the IBM’s clock. Most of the rules below follow from that: where the two models can be made to agree, they should agree by construction, not by fitting.

fleet is a work in progress and not ready for real use; see the README.

Generated code

inst/odin/malaria_daily.R is the model source; src/malaria_daily.cpp is what runs. The C++ is generated from the odin source and committed to the repository. If you edit the odin file and do not regenerate, everything still passes: R CMD check compiles the old model, the tests exercise the old model, and the drift check reports that nothing moved, which reads as a numerically inert change rather than one that was never compiled.

After any edit to inst/odin/malaria_daily.R, regenerate:

odin2::odin_package(".")

and commit the regenerated files with the change:

src/malaria_daily.cpp   src/cpp11.cpp   R/dust.R   R/cpp11.R   inst/dust/malaria_daily.cpp

The generated-code job in .github/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml regenerates the code on Linux and fails on any difference. odin2 prints a fractional literal to 17 digits, which differs between platforms unless the number is a short binary fraction: 0.5 is safe, 1e-12 is not. Write any other constant as a quotient of whole numbers, 1 / 1e12, which prints the same everywhere; test-odin-literals.R checks this locally.

Setup

install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_deps(dependencies = TRUE)

None of the seven modelling dependencies (odin2, dust2, monty, malariaEquilibrium, malariaEquilibriumVivax, malariasimulation, postie) is on CRAN. Remotes in DESCRIPTION points them at GitHub, which is where install_deps() fetches them from. A C++ toolchain is required (Rtools on Windows).

Tests

devtools::test()

The suite requires malariasimulation. It errors rather than skips if that package is missing, so that a runner that cannot build the IBM fails instead of reporting success having tested almost nothing. Set FLEET_ALLOW_SKIP=1 to skip instead, locally only.

devtools::load_all() and devtools::test() compile the model with debug flags (-O0), which makes it about ten times slower, and leave those object files in src/. R CMD INSTALL on the source directory then reuses them, so an install made after load_all() is the slow build without saying so. Install with R CMD INSTALL --preclean ., or delete src/*.o first, before timing anything.

Changing the model

Two committed baselines pin fleet’s output, so a deliberate model change means refreshing both and reading both diffs.

The first is this repository’s reference values, which pin absolute output levels to 1e-6: tests/testthat/reference-values.csv, reference-interventions.csv, reference-vivax.csv and reference-vivax-interventions.csv. Regenerate them against a fresh R CMD INSTALL:

FLEET_REGENERATE_REFERENCE=1 Rscript -e 'testthat::test_file("tests/testthat/test-reference.R", package = "fleet", load_package = "installed")'

The second is the committed fleet rows in fleetcheck, the separate repository that compares fleet with the IBM. A change that moves model output moves these too, so refresh them in the same change: clone fleetcheck beside this repository and run CMP_FLEET_ONLY=1 Rscript validations/02-scenarios/run.R, then validations/02-scenarios/render.R. For a change that reaches the vivax block, repeat with CMP_PARASITE=pv, then render_pv.R. The IBM rows do not need re-running, since nothing in fleet can affect them, so this takes minutes rather than the hours of a full sweep.

Never regenerate a baseline to make a failing test pass. The diff is the record of what your change did to the model: read it, and include it in the pull request.

Model conventions

  • Replicate malariasimulation exactly. Where the IBM has a known mechanism, mirror it, including its per-day discretisation and its arithmetic. Mean-matched approximations and fudge factors are not accepted, even when they improve agreement. If the mean field cannot carry a mechanism, document the departure and measure it rather than tuning around it.
  • Cite the source. Most mean-field choices name the malariasimulation file and line they mirror; keep doing so, as it is what makes a divergence auditable later.
  • Deliberate departures carry their evidence. bite_dedup and acquired_immunity_offset both exist because an A/B measurement justified them, and both record it.
  • set_equilibrium() must be the last call on a parameter list. It stores eq_params, which freezes the translated biological constants, so edits made afterwards are ignored. fleet warns when it detects this.

Pull requests

  • Branch from main and keep changes focused.
  • State what moved. If output changed, include the baseline diff and explain it.
  • New behaviour needs a test that fails without the change. For anything that touches model output, that means an absolute assertion, not only a relation: a test that checks that output with an intervention is below output without it still passes if the whole output is multiplied by a constant.
  • Documentation is part of the change. If a change falsifies a claim in the README or a vignette, fix it in the same pull request.

Reporting a problem

Open an issue with your sessionInfo(), the fleet commit, and a reproducible example. For anything numerical, say which parameter list you used and how you seeded it.
